# On the Art of Paying Attention

There's a peculiar tyranny in modern life—the assumption that everything is equally available to us, and therefore equally unimportant. We live in the strange paradox of abundance where nothing feels precious. We have access to nearly all human knowledge, art, and music, yet find ourselves scrolling past masterpieces without pausing. We're surrounded by remarkable people and moments, yet feel profoundly alone. I think this comes down to attention, and how we've collectively forgotten that attention is the rarest currency we possess.

I was reminded of this recently while sitting in a café, watching a woman across from me. She wasn't doing anything extraordinary—just reading a book, occasionally looking out the window, sipping her coffee. But she was *present*. Not in the Instagram sense of being mindfully present, but genuinely inhabiting her moment. No phone on the table. No checking. Just her, the book, the coffee, the ambient noise of the café. I realized I was envying her in the most basic way: the ability to do one thing at a time without the invisible weight of a thousand other things pressing against her attention.

When did we collectively decide that divided attention was acceptable? I suspect it happened gradually, the way most significant cultural shifts do. A smartphone here, a notification there, until suddenly we're all operating in a state of perpetual partial attention—never fully here, never fully anywhere. We're trained now to feel that not checking our messages is a small act of resistance, something to be proud of. We've normalized inattention to such a degree that the simple act of finishing a book without picking up your phone has become a meditation practice.

The philosopher Simone Weil wrote about attention as something sacred. She believed that true attention was the rarest form of generosity—when you truly attend to another person, you're giving them the most valuable thing you have: your presence. Not your presence as in "being in the same room," but the whole architecture of your consciousness turned toward them. This kind of attention has become increasingly rare, and I suspect we're all suffering from its absence, even if we don't have language for it.

I think about writers, particularly those from before the internet age. How strange it must have been, in some ways, to work knowing there would be no immediate feedback loop. You would finish a novel, send it out into the world, and wait months or years to hear anything. There was a kind of spaciousness to that—time to think, to revise, to sit with your own work without the anxiety of real-time validation or criticism. Now we're all writing into the void of the internet, where attention is the economy and every work is immediately quantified by how many views or likes or shares it received.

This changes how we create, I think. Not always for the worse, but it changes the fundamental relationship between the maker and the work. When I write now, some part of me is calculating—will this be interesting enough? Will it hook people in the first sentence? It's hard to quiet that voice, that awareness of the attention marketplace. The artists I know who seem most at peace are the ones who have somehow managed to retreat from this economy. Not completely—they still need to eat, still hope their work finds an audience—but they've carved out some protected space where they create without constantly checking how it's being received.

I've been thinking too about what we lose when we lose deep attention. There's a quality of thinking that only becomes available when you've been with an idea, a problem, a text for an extended period. The mathematician Andrew Wiles spent seven years working on Fermat's Last Theorem in secret, essentially alone with the problem. He describes it as entering a landscape, becoming familiar with its contours, knowing it so intimately that solutions would sometimes come to him in dreams. This kind of thinking—deep, immersive, sustained—seems increasingly impossible in a world designed to interrupt us every few minutes.

I notice this in how I read. I can no longer read the way I did as a teenager—for hours without surface-level awareness, sinking into a book as though it were quicksand. Now I'm hyperaware of my reading: Have I been reading too long? Should I be doing something else? The book, the reading, myself reading, and a kind of meta-awareness of all of it. It's like trying to fall asleep while being simultaneously aware of yourself trying to fall asleep. The attention fragments under the weight of its own self-consciousness.

Yet I also notice that I don't actually want to go backward. I don't fantasize about a pre-internet world in any serious way. The connectivity, the access, the ability to find and communicate with people across the world—these are genuine goods. The problem isn't technology itself, it's the way attention has been weaponized by the technology. Or perhaps more precisely, the way our attention has been turned into a product to be harvested and sold. Every app, every interface, is designed by people whose explicit goal is to capture and keep your attention. It's not a bug; it's the business model. You're not using the product; you are the product.

What would it look like to reclaim attention as something that belongs to us? I don't think it requires abandoning technology or retreating to some romantic past. But it might require deliberate, intentional choices about where our attention goes. It might require saying no more often—no to notifications, no to checking, no to the constant invitation to be elsewhere.

I've been experimenting with this. Setting my phone down for hours at a time. Implementing a rule where I don't check email in the morning. Reading physical books again. What I've noticed is that the first phase is uncomfortable—there's a genuine itch, an anxiety about what I might be missing. But if I push past that, something interesting happens. The attention settles. The background noise quiets. Whatever I'm doing—writing, reading, thinking—starts to feel like it matters because I'm actually there for it.

There's a concept in Buddhism called "bare attention"—the ability to perceive things as they actually are without immediately filtering them through judgment, categorization, or habit. I wonder if we could apply this to our daily lives. What if we attended to our breakfast with bare attention? Actually tasted the coffee, noticed the texture of the toast, the quality of light on the table? What if we attended to our conversations this way, truly hearing what the other person said rather than waiting for our turn to speak?

I suspect we would find our lives much richer. Not because nothing would change externally, but because the quality of our experience would increase dramatically. There's a poverty of the soul that comes from constant distraction, a kind of emptiness that we keep trying to fill by seeking more distraction. It's a vicious cycle, and I'm not sure how to break it except one moment at a time.

This connects to something I think about often: the relationship between boredom and creativity. We're afraid of boredom now. We treat it like a disease to be prevented at all costs. But boredom, real boredom—not the boredom of scrolling through your phone, but the boredom of sitting with your own thoughts, of having time stretch out before you without anything to do—this is where creativity lives. The blank mind is fertile ground. Most of our ideas, our insights, our moments of genuine inspiration come when we're not trying, when we're bored in the best sense of the word.

Children get bored and then they invent elaborate games. Writers talk about being bored as the source of their work. Musicians describe getting stuck on a phrase and letting it live in their boredom until something breaks open. But we don't give ourselves or our children that space anymore. Every moment is optimized, scheduled, filled. We're so busy being productive that we don't have time to think about whether what we're producing is worth anything.

I watched a documentary recently about people who work in digital distraction—designers, engineers, product managers at social media companies. What struck me was how many of them don't let their own children use the products they create. They keep phones and tablets away from their kids. They're aware, in a way that users might not be, of what these technologies do to attention and development. There's something darkly comic about it—and something tragic.

The attention economy will probably only get more sophisticated. Virtual reality, artificial intelligence, whatever's coming next—these will likely be designed with even more sophisticated hooks into our attention. So the question becomes: what do we do about it? Do we accept it as inevitable? Do we fight it?

I think the answer is somewhere in between. I think we need to be realistic about how compelling these technologies are—they're not compelling because they're evil, but because they tap into genuine human desires for connection, knowledge, stimulation. We need to work with human nature, not against it. But we also need to be intentional and protective about where our attention goes, the way we might be protective about what we feed our bodies.

This means making choices that might feel countercultural. Turning off notifications. Having phone-free times and spaces. Reading books without tabs open. Sitting with people and not checking messages. These small acts are becoming small rebellions, and I'm not sure whether to find that funny or sad. That paying attention has become a form of resistance—against our own devices, against corporations, against the zeitgeist.

But I do find something hopeful in it too. When I'm with a friend and neither of us have our phones out, when we're actually *talking*, I feel something that I otherwise miss. A kind of human connection that feels real and grounding. When I'm deep in a book, hours have passed and I haven't noticed, and there's a kind of joy in that absorption, that loss of self in something beyond myself. When I'm writing and the words are coming and I'm not thinking about how they'll be received, just following the thought wherever it goes—these moments feel like life actually happening, rather than a performance of life.

Maybe that's what this is really about. Not the technology itself, but whether we're living our lives or performing them. Whether we're present for our own existence or watching it from a distance, always aware of how it looks, what people might think, whether it's worth posting. That's the real cost of divided attention—not that we're less productive or less informed, but that we become strangers to our own lives.

So I'm trying to pay attention. To the people in front of me. To my own thoughts when they come. To the world, which is genuinely remarkable if you actually look at it. To the work that matters to me, without constantly checking whether it matters to anyone else. It's harder than it should be, which tells you something about where we are culturally. But it's also, I think, one of the most important things any of us can do right now.

We're not going to solve the attention economy. We're not going to opt out entirely. But we can reclaim small spaces of genuine presence, genuine focus, genuine care for what we're doing and who we're with. We can treat attention as the precious thing it is—not as a resource to be maximized and monetized, but as the fundamental currency of a meaningful life. That seems worth paying attention to.
